articles.title: World Series 2026: Jackson Chourio ties Babe Ruth for most hits in first 4 games of a Fall Classic
articles.summary: Chourio recorded his ninth and 10th hits of this series in Milwaukee's Game 4 loss.
articles.body:
With the Milwaukee Brewers holding a 3-2 lead in the top of the 12th inning of Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday, Jackson Chourio came to the plate with a chance to put his name next to a legend's.

Chourio hit a two-out double off of Tampa Bay Rays reliever Ian Seymour. With that, he secured his 10th hit of the World Series, which tied Babe Ruth for the most by a player in the first four games of a Fall Classic.

Ruth's record had stood as his own since 1928. He secured his tally across a 4-0 New York Yankees sweep of the St. Louis Cardinals.

Chourio's hit continued a remarkable run for the 22-year-old slugger, who has been a threat in Milwaukee's lineup for the entirety of his three-season MLB career. He entered Game 4 slashing .286/.308/.429 this postseason with 2 home runs, 9 RBI and 3 stolen bases. He finished Tuesday's game 2-for-6 at the plate.

His 10th-inning hit was his 16th this postseason and his 31st through three postseasons. That moved him past Atlanta Braves Hall of Famer Andruw Jones for the most postseason hits by a player before turning 23. Chourio reached his tally in 21 fewer games than Jones.

Milwaukee took a 3-2 lead in the top of the 12th via a Cooper Pratt solo home run. But the Rays tied the game and loaded the bases with no outs in the bottom of the 12th.

Then Ben Williamson delivered a walk-off RBI single to secure a 4-3 Tampa Bay victory to fend off a sweep and cut Milwaukee's series lead to 3-1.

Game 5 is scheduled for 8 p.m. ET Wednesday in St. Petersburg.

articles.title: Rays' Nick Martinez Says Team is 'Capable' of Historic World Series Comeback After Walk-Off G4 Win
articles.summary: After keeping their season alive with a dramatic 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in 12 innings in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday night, the Tampa Bay Rays got the glimmer of hope they need to believe a historic comeback is possible.
articles.body:
After keeping their season alive with a dramatic 4-3 victory over the Milwaukee Brewers in 12 innings in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday night, the Tampa Bay Rays got the glimmer of hope they need to believe a historic comeback is possible.

Rays pitcher Nick Martinez told reporters after the win they are "capable" of becoming the first team in World Series history to overcome a 3-0 series deficit.

"Sometimes you just got to see one through," said Martinez, who pitched two scoreless innings in relief. "We can win four in a row. This team is capable of doing that."

The Brewers, who have been the comeback kids throughout this postseason, got to experience it from the other side when Tampa scored twice in the bottom of the 12th to get the win after Cooper Pratt put the NL champs up 3-2 in the top of the frame.

Milwaukee's loss snapped its eight-game playoff winning streak that was tied for the longest by any team in MLB history.

The most famous eight-game postseason win streak was the 2004 Boston Red Sox, who are still the only team to overcome a 3-0 deficit in a best-of-seven series in MLB history. They won four straight against the New York Yankees in the ALCS, then swept the St. Louis Cardinals in the World Series.

Tampa only has to win four straight games to capture its first championship. It would be a Herculean task if the Rays pull it off, but the first hurdle has been cleared.

The Brewers did have two losing streaks of at least four games in the regular season, though both of them came back in April.

Milwaukee will send Jacob Misiorowski to the mound in Game 5 on Wednesday at 8 p.m. ET looking to clinch its first World Series title in franchise history.

The Rays have not yet announced their starting pitcher. Martinez, who started Game 1, would have been in line to take the mound if he had not been used on Tuesday.

articles.title: Brewers' Christian Yelich Sounds Off on World Series G4 Loss, 'Not Supposed to Be Easy'
articles.summary: Outfielder and team captain Christian Yelich summed things up following the Milwaukee Brewers' heartbreaking, 4-3 loss in extra innings to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday.
articles.body:
Outfielder and team captain Christian Yelich summed things up following the Milwaukee Brewers' heartbreaking, 4-3 loss in extra innings to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 4 of the World Series on Tuesday.

Speaking to reporters after the Brewers allowed a golden opportunity to close out the series to slip through their fingers, Yelich said, "This stuff is not supposed to be easy. It's supposed to test you."

Trailing by scores of 1-0 and 2-1, the Brewers twice battled back to tie things up in Game 4 thanks to an RBI double by Cooper Pratt and solo home run by David Hamilton.

That allowed Milwaukee to force extra innings, and after the teams failed to score in the 10th and 11th innings, Pratt smacked a solo homer in the top of the 12th to put the Brewers ahead 3-2.

Milwaukee entered the bottom of the 12th needing three outs to win the first World Series in franchise history, but things went awry from there.

After Junior Caminero began the inning by reaching first base on a throwing error by Joey Ortiz, Shane Drohan entered the game and allowed four consecutive singles.

An RBI single by Jonny DeLuca tied it, and a walk-off RBI single by Ben Williamson won it, thus giving the Rays new life.

The Brewers still have a huge advantage, up 3-2 with likely National League Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski set to take the mound in Game 5 on Wednesday, but it is fair to wonder if losing Game 4 in such dramatic fashion could potentially mess with the Brew Crew's psyche.

articles.title: Fans debate Brewers decision to keep Jacob Misiorowski in dugout with chance to win first ever World Series
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers were three outs from a World Series sweep before Pat Murphy's decision to hold Jacob Misiorowski sparked fierce debate.
articles.body: It is hardly a new phenomenon to see starting pitchers - elite ones at that - get the final outs of the World Series, but the Milwaukee Brewers passed on that opportunity. Up 3-2 heading into the bottom of the 12th, the Brewers were three outs away from a sweep to win their first Fall Classic. Having used up plenty of relievers, manager Pat Murphy decided to keep impending Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski in the dugout and go with Shane Drohan. But Drohan, who got bitten by his defense, did not record an out, and a Game 5 will be played Wednesday night. "You can't blow that type of situation on a one-run lead on the road," Murphy said. "If we were in the 13th inning and had a three-run lead, that might be a little bit different, and I probably still wouldn't have." The move was highly debated on social media in the early morning hours after the game. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "Not sure it gets as utter woke nonsense as saving the best pitcher in the world for a hypothetical game 5 where you’d still be up 3-1," said another. "Wouldn’t have needed a game 5 , congrats on out thinking yourself," added one more. And, of course, there's the contrary. YANKEES LEGEND SAYS HE DOES NOT 'FEEL WELCOME' BY TEAM DESPITE LEGENDARY CAREER "They had 3-0 game lead. No reason to throw Misiorowski in this game," one opposer said. "What if he had and Tampa still won. He would have lost him for at least game 5," a Rays fan wrote. Misiorowski pitched to an MLB-leading 1.80 ERA this season, and his 252 strikeouts and 13.0 K/9 were also league bests . He has not found similar success in October, but he's still fared quite nicely (2.70 ERA, 14 strikeouts in 13.1 innings spanning three starts). Had Misiorowski blown the save (an unlikely scenario), who knows who would pitch Game 5, but it's hard to imagine that he would not be available in a necessary Game 6 at home. Murphy went with seven relievers after starter Dustin May tossed just three innings. Trevor Megill was used for one batter in the eighth inning, and Aaron Ashby, who has now allowed a run in 18.0 innings, started the ninth and was taken out after recording one out in the 11th. articles.title: Yankees legend Jorge Posada says he doesn't 'feel welcome' around the team anymore
articles.summary: Jorge Posada spent all 17 of his MLB seasons with the Yankees.
articles.body:
Throughout the New York Yankees' late-'90s dynasty, few players epitomized the team better than Jorge Posada. His rise to prominence coincided with the Yankees' three-peat during the decade. From there, he remained a mainstay in the lineup over his 17-year MLB career.

Now, he no longer feels welcome around the team. Posada revealed that information during an appearance on the New York Post's baseball podcast.

When asked whether he would be a good candidate to help the team's coaching staff, Posada said, "I could, but I don't think they want me there to tell you the truth."

When asked why he believed that was the case, Posada followed up:

"I don't feel welcome when I go there. Even in spring training, I don't feel like … I don't feel welcome. I don't feel like they want me there, so I don't go."

Posada said he wasn't sure what caused his relationship with the team to change and expressed a desire to move forward. He added, however, that the final year of his career was difficult, and it's tough to relive those feelings when he returns to the team.

After 14 fantastic years as a mainstay with the team, Posada saw his numbers dip in his final year with the Yankees. Relegated to the team's designated hitter role, Posada hit just .235/.315/.398 in his final year. He was 40.

A few months later, he retired. Despite the Yankees not showing interest in bringing him back for another year, Posada retired as a member of the franchise and spoke highly of the Yankees during his retirement announcement.

While the Yankees have turned in some strong seasons since Posada's retirement, making the playoffs in 10 of 14 tries, the team hasn't won a World Series during that stretch. Despite a sense that things have stalled out under manager Aaron Boone, the team announced in October that he would be back as its manager for another season.

With Boone back, there's a belief the Yankees could benefit from some new blood elsewhere in the organization. Posada could provide that, and his word could carry some weight in the clubhouse considering his history with the organization.

For now, that type of role doesn't appear in the cards for Posada, at least not until he feels more welcome around his former team.

articles.title: New Mets Rumors on Teruaki Sato Reveal David Stearns' Scouting Trip After MLB Season
articles.summary: With Teruaki Sato set to be arguably the most sought-after position player in free agency, the New York Mets look like a team to monitor for the Japanese star.
articles.body:
With Teruaki Sato set to be arguably the most sought-after position player in free agency, the New York Mets look like a team to monitor for the Japanese star.

Per Chelsea Janes of SNY, president of baseball operations David Stearns went to Japan "as soon as the Mets' season ended" specifically to watch the Sato play for the Hanshin Tigers.

"You don't make that trip if you aren't seriously considering making a push for him," Janes wrote.

Hanshin announced on Oct. 19 that Sato would be posted for MLB teams this offseason. The 27-year-old is not subject to international free-agent rules, giving him a 45-day window to negotiate a deal without financial restrictions with all 30 MLB clubs after he is posted.

MLB.com's Mark Feinsand ranked Sato as the top position player and No. 4 overall free agent in the upcoming class, behind Tarik Skubal, Michael King and Freddy Peralta.

According to Feinsand, Sato has drawn comparisons to Munetaka Murakami thanks to his prodigious power and high strikeout totals. He has hit 79 homers and struck out 327 times in 1,211 plate appearances over the past two seasons in NPB.

Murakami came to MLB with big questions about his ability to make contact, which likely led to him signing a lower-than-expected deal with the Chicago White Sox for $34 million over two years.

The strikeout issues for Murakami weren't proven wrong with 196 in 553 plate appearances this season, but he also walked enough to post a .347 on-base percentage and slugged 35 homers to help the White Sox make a surprise playoff appearance.

Sato figures to benefit from Murakami's success, as well as being arguably the best power bat available in a soft free-agent class. Randy Arozarena, Seiya Suzuki, Jake Bauers and Brandon Lowe are the other notable position players who can hit the market.

Stearns is already under an intense microscope from fans in Queens after the Mets missed the playoffs for the second consecutive seasons. Their 74-88 record this year was their worst in a 162-game season since 2017 (70-92).

After having the highest payroll in MLB in 2026, the Mets aren't going to get much contract relief unless they make some trades. Bo Bichette and Chris Devenski are their only potential free agents.

Bo Bichette could opt out of his deal worth $42 million in 2027, but his struggles this season would seem to make it unlikely he decides to test the market this offseason, particularly given the labor uncertainty with the current CBA set to expire on Dec. 1.

Mets owner Steve Cohen has not shied away from aggressively spending in the interest of improving the roster.

If Cohen believes Sato can be a difference-maker that gets them back to being competitive in the NL East, it wouldn't be a surprise if the five-time NPB All-Star signs with the Mets.

articles.title: Drew Rasmussen to Start World Series G5 on Short Rest with Rays Facing Elimination vs. Brewers
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays will start Drew Rasmussen in Wednesday's Game 5, according to Marc Topkin of the Tampa Bay Times, as the team tries to move another step closer to pulling off the rare reverse-sweep following Tuesday night's 12th-inning victory.
articles.body:
The Tampa Bay Rays will start Drew Rasmussen in Wednesday's Game 5, according to Marc Topkin of the Tampa Bay Times , as the team tries to move another step closer to pulling off the rare reverse-sweep following Tuesday night's 12th-inning victory.

Rasmussen started Game 2 on Saturday and will be pitching on just three days rest. Rays manager Kevin Cash revealed he was up until four in the morning following his team's Game 4 win to prepare pitching plans for Game 5.

He didn't fare well in that contest, giving up three runs on six hits and two walks in 3.2 innings while striking out four. He threw 89 pitches in the contest. The Rays ultimately lost, 5-4, despite scoring four runs in the top of the first.

The Rays are very much in an all-hands-on-deck situation now, especially after requiring seven pitchers to get through Tuesday's 4-3 win. That included Game 1 starter Nick Martinez, who threw two innings in the victory.

Meanwhile Milwaukee will trot out ace Jacob Misiorowski. The Brewers used eight pitchers during Game 4, so getting a long outing from Misiorowski would be ideal, though he's only thrown 13.1 innings across three postseason games thus far, averaging 86 pitches per contest.

He does have a 2.70 ERA with 14 strikeouts and no homers allowed in those outings, however, and the Brewers have won all three games.

On paper, Misiorowski vs. Rasmussen on short rest is a pretty heavy mismatch in favor of the Brewers. But October baseball has a way of defying expectations.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Rays to start ace Drew Rasmussen in Game 5 with season on the line
articles.summary: Drew Rasmussen turned in his second straight All-Star season in 2026.
articles.body:
With their season on the line Wednesday, the Tampa Bay Rays will turn to ace Drew Rasmussen on three days rest to keep the team alive another day. Hours before game time, the team announced Rasmussen would draw the start in Game 5 of the World Series.

It will mark Rasmussen's first start since Game 2 on Saturday, when he allowed three runs over 3 2/3 innings against the Milwaukee Brewers. The Rays were able to get to Brewers starter Logan Henderson in that contest, so Rasmussen actually left Game 2 with a one-run lead.

The Rays' bullpen couldn't hold that lead, however, eventually losing Game 2 to fall behind 2-0 in the series.

Following their win in Game 4 on Tuesday, the Rays need to win out in order to take down the Brewers and win the 2026 World Series.

Doing so will require some fantastic pitching over the next three games. In that sense, going with Rasmussen is probably the best strategy. He was the team's best pitcher in the regular season, posting a 2.67 ERA over 170 innings. That performance was good enough to earn Rasmussen his second straight All-Star nod.

But the team is taking a significant risk by putting Rasmussen on the mound. The 31-year-old will not only pitch on short rest, but will need to give the Rays as much length as possible after the team burned through seven pitchers in Tuesday's Game 4 win and six pitchers in Monday's Game 3 loss.

While the Rays will likely be willing to use anyone in Game 5, the team runs the risk of sending a fatigued and overtaxed pitcher on the mound at any moment, a dangerous gambit for a team one mistake away from losing the World Series.

Though Rasmussen struggled in Game 2 vs. the Brewers, he had previously been excellent this postseason. In his three previous starts during these playoffs, Rasmussen had a 1.29 ERA and 23 strikeouts over 21 innings.

articles.title: Mark Walter Won't Sell Dodgers 'No Matter What' After Lakers Sale, Reiterates Commitment to Winning
articles.summary: While he has divested himself from a big chunk of his sports portfolio, Mark Walter has no plans to sell his stake in the Los Angeles Dodgers.
articles.body:
While he has divested himself from a big chunk of his sports portfolio, Mark Walter has no plans to sell his stake in the Los Angeles Dodgers.

"We're going to keep the team no matter what," he told the California Post's Jack Harris . "We're going to be winning for 10 years or more. I think our commitment to do so will be just like it has been in the past. And, you know, we don't win every year, but we're going to try to."

In August, Walter brokered a deal to sell the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion after having purchased the franchise from the Buss family less than a year earlier. His brief spell in charge raised bigger questions about his ownership stakes elsewhere.

Dodgers president Stan Kasten quickly reiterated the team wasn't for sale.

Walter did, however, cash in on his investment in Premier League club Chelsea, and Bloomberg's Randall Williams, Sridhar Natarajan, and Lucas Shaw reported last week the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks could be next.

Walter declined to comment on that report in his interview with Harris.

The 66-year-old was part of the ownership group (Guggenheim Baseball Management) that purchased the Dodgers in 2012 from Frank McCourt. The team has since enjoyed its longest sustained spell of success ever.

Los Angeles stretched its playoff streak to 14 seasons in 2026 and has three World Series titles during the Guggenheim Baseball Management. The Dodgers have perfected the team-building blueprint, combining big payrolls with elite player development.

Some cracks might be starting to emerge, though. Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow and Will Smith are all on the wrong side of 30. Signing Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz look like an expensive mistakes.

Every dynasty ends at some point. The Dodgers aren't there yet , but they look as mortal as they have in a long time.

An ownership change would present a big variable to the franchise at an inopportune time.

articles.title: Yankees president Randy Levine says he is 'confident' MLB will avoid a lockout despite cap fight
articles.summary: World Series Game 5 could be MLB's last game for the foreseeable future as the CBA expires Dec. 1 and owners push for a salary cap in baseball.
articles.body: Game 5 of the World Series could very well be the last baseball game for the foreseeable future. The league's current collective bargaining agreement with the players expires on Dec. 1, and the players and owners appear as far apart as they ever have been. Assuming there is no deal, the owners are expected to lock out the players, as was the case five years ago which led to the season being delayed by one week. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Despite the apparently harsh circumstances at the moment, New York Yankees president Randy Levine is actually "confident" things will all work out. "It's very, very early... They want to reach an agreement. It's always this way in every labor negotiation I've done. It's always posturing at this point in time, getting your position out," Levine said on "The Craig Carton Show." "We have until December. I think they're really going to work hard, and I'm very hopeful they'll reach an agreement. I've seen circumstances where it looked harder than even this, and this one looks hard, but at the end of the day, I'm confident everyone wants to get a deal." "The whole playoffs have been great, the whole season has been great. Baseball is regaining popularity, it's the national pastime, so we gotta work hard to just preserve it," Levine added. Levine's boss, Hal Steinbrenner, said last week he "support[s]" the owners' proposals — all of which include a cap. "I've said before — let me put it this way, as a member of the labor policy committee — I helped craft, one of many, the proposals that we have given at the bargaining table. And I support those proposals in their entirety. That's absolutely the case, so that should answer your question," Steinbrenner told reporters. The Yankees' $336 million payroll was the third-largest in baseball during the 2026 season, behind the Los Angeles Dodgers ($422 million) and New York Mets ($338 million). FANS DEBATE BREWERS DECISION TO KEEP JACOB MISIOROWSKI IN DUGOUT WITH CHANCE TO WIN FIRST EVER WORLD SERIES Arguments skew both ways, but a constant has remained in that the highest payrolls continue to go up, while the lowest payrolls remain at a stall. The Marlins' payroll is actually roughly half of what it used to be in 2017, despite a sale of the team and everyone in the league making more money than ever. Meanwhile, the Dodgers have already committed more money in 2030 than 12 teams have this season. MLB commissioner Rob Manfred has said that owners are simply "listening to our fans" regarding a salary cap and said it "defies human experience... to think that the bottom end of that [payroll] gap has the same opportunity to win the top end." It should be noted, though, that the National League-winning Milwaukee Brewers swept the Dodgers with the 11th-smallest payroll, and they are facing the Tampa Bay Rays, who have the league's third-smallest payroll. They defeated the Cleveland Guardians, who rank 29th in payroll, in the American League Division Series. Major League Baseball has never had a salary cap. "Salary cap is the ultimate excuse not to compete. It's the ultimate excuse for an owner to say, 'Gee, I would like to make the team better, but you know I can’t,'" interim MLBPA executive director Bruce Meyer said during the All-Star break. "Salary caps are bad for fans. Salary caps prevent teams from doing the things that they believe are in their interest to make the team better." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Every team in baseball can afford to compete, many are choosing not to," Meyer added. "To me, that's the biggest problem right now."

articles.title: Key dates & storylines as Mets approach offseason
articles.summary: When the World Series concludes, the Mets can start to get a move on in their offseason. In what is expected to be a turbulent winter, the Mets don’t have an...
articles.body:
When the World Series concludes, the Mets can start to get a move on in their offseason.

In what is expected to be a turbulent winter, the Mets don't have an immense amount of business to take care of before the expected lockout on Dec. 1. They traded away the veterans who were on expiring contracts at the deadline over the summer and installed a manager, Andy Green , before the end of the regular season. The club is looking to make some minor changes to the coaching staff after firing hitting coach Jeff Albert, and in the front office, where the team is seeking a farm director to replace Green.

Here are key dates and storylines to watch for as the offseason approaches.

After the commissioner's trophy is awarded, a five-day "quiet period" begins where pending free agents can negotiate with their current teams. Bo Bichette is the only potential free agent for the Mets. The third baseman has a player option for 2027 and one for 2028, and will have five days from the conclusion of the World Series to make a decision.

Late in the season, Bichette sounded as though he was leaning toward staying in Queens, but nothing is final.

It was an uncharacteristic season for the infielder. He played third base for the first time, though he was moved back to his natural shortstop position for a few months while Francisco Lindor was on the injured list. He hit just .260, though he matched his 2025 home run total with 18.

Bichette, 28, often lamented his inability to come through for the team in the first half, saying if he had, the Mets might have been in a better position. A good teammate with a strong work ethic, the Mets want him back. With the lockout looming, it might benefit him to take the option for next season instead of trying to feel out free agency for the second year in a row.

Free agents can negotiate with other teams after the quiet period ends. The biggest name on the market is Los Angeles Dodgers ace and two-time Cy Young Award winner Tarik Skubal. The Mets, in need of starting pitching, should do what they can to sign the lefty.

The GM Meetings used to be a quiet affair. Rule changes were discussed at resorts around various Southwestern cities. It's where executives used to lay the framework for roster building, discussing things in broad terms and doing initial check-ins on items they would later circle back to at the Winter Meetings.

That isn't the case this season. The meetings have moved to Las Vegas for the foreseeable future, a city that is anything but quiet, and they now precede the MLB Awards Show, a full-blown red-carpet affair. The Winter Meetings will be canceled if the league locks out the players, so teams are expected to meet with players in Las Vegas instead of waiting until December.

NOV. 17: DEADLINE TO ACCEPT QUALIFYING OFFERS

Eligible players have until 4 p.m. ET to accept or reject the qualifying offer.

The final date for teams to offer a contract to all arbitration-eligible and pre-arbitration players on their 40-man roster for next season; this is where the Mets have some tough decisions to make. Their list of arbitration-eligible players is long: Mark Vientos, Brett Baty, Francisco Alvarez, Ronny Mauricio, Tylor Megill, Reed Garrett, Robert Stock and Austin Warren.

Vientos, Baty, Alvarez and Mauricio were once top prospects in the Mets' system, but they aren't prospects anymore.

Alvarez, a power-hitting catcher, was primarily the Mets' full-time catcher until this season, when his defense was so poor the team had to use Luis Torrens as the main backstop. Injuries are also a concern for Alvarez, who has spent significant time on the injured list in each of the last three seasons. But he's a well-liked, well-respected catcher, and it's tough to let someone with his power go.

Though it's clear the pop is still there, Vientos doesn't have a full-time position, and he's struggled as a platoon hitter over the last two seasons. The Mets converted Baty, a third baseman, to a super utility role this season, using him at first base and in the outfield in addition to second and third base. Though his outfield defense was particularly lacking, the Mets were happy with how he approached the season and the professionalism he showed in embracing a new challenge.

It's tough to know what to do with Mauricio. The time he lost from his knee injury clearly stunted his development; he's struggled to hit breaking balls at the big-league level, and he's out of minor league options. But the switch-hitter can seriously impact the baseball and play multiple infield positions. Veteran infielders Lindor and Marcus Semien both spent time on the IL last season, and they aren't getting any younger, so keeping him around next season might be beneficial.

For the second time in five years, the 30 club owners are expected to lock out their players. All activity involving players on 40-man rosters will halt. Players and teams cannot communicate until a new CBA is agreed upon and ratified.
authors: Abbey Mastracco, New York Daily News

articles.title: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy may have cost his team a chance to clinch the World Series
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy chose Shane Drohan over Jacob Misiorowski with three outs left, and the World Series Game 4 lead vanished.
articles.body: Until late Tuesday night, the Milwaukee Brewers coasted through the 2026 Major League Baseball playoffs. They had won eight straight games against the San Diego Padres, Los Angeles Dodgers and Tampa Bay Rays. The hottest team in baseball in the second half of the season, a high-powered, star-studded, expensive roster that won 100 games, and the best team in the American League that also won 98 games. It seemed like every single move manager Pat Murphy made worked perfectly. Better than perfectly. When they started light-hitting utility infielder David Hamilton, he hit a home run off Edwin Diaz to give the Brewers an insurance run in the ninth inning of a clinching Game 4 in the NLCS. Sal Frelick was perfectly positioned to run down a 106 mph line drive to right center field off the bat of Freddie Freeman, potentially changing the course of game two. RAYS STAY ALIVE IN WORLD SERIES, WALK OFF BREWERS IN THRILLING EXTRA-INNING GAME 4 Aaron Ashby, a very good reliever, had become the best reliever in postseason history. Better than Mariano Rivera, better than Kenley Jansen, or Billy Wagner, or other elite pitchers. His 18 scoreless innings to start a postseason set a new baseball record. Robert Gasser, an average to below average starter, had allowed just one run in 15 innings, despite getting few swings and misses or strikeouts. In Game 4 of the World Series, Hamilton, who had just four homers in the regular season, hit another one to tie the score at two. Then rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt hit a go-ahead homer in the top of the 12th inning, putting the Brewers three outs away from clinching their first ever championship. If that doesn't sum up Milwaukee's postseason run, it's hard to imagine what would. But in the bottom of the 12th, it all fell apart in the blink of an eye. Junior Caminero reached on an error. Liam Hicks singled, sending Caminero to third. Jonny DeLuca tied it with a single to center. Chandler Simpson singled to load the bases. Then Ben Williamson ended it with a very Brewers-like hit, a ground ball to the right side that took a huge bounce over first base to reach the outfield. Innings like that happen all the time in baseball. An error to start the inning, followed by things quickly spiraling. There are a few well-placed hits, a lucky bounce goes the opposing team's way, and before you know it, two runs have scored and the game is over. But what made this outcome especially frustrating for Milwaukee was that it might not have needed to happen. Drohan hadn't pitched since Oct. 15, when he gave up a run to the Dodgers in the NLCS. He'd pitched in a competitive game just once in the past month. At first glance Murphy had few other choices, as all of his best relievers had already been used. Aaron Ashby went over two innings. Trevor Megill was used for just one out. DL Hall had pitched, as had Abner Uribe and JoJo Romero. And it's easy to second guess, knowing the outcome, but there was one other option to get the final three outs against the heart of the Tampa Bay lineup: the likely NL Cy Young Award winner, Jacob Misiorowski. Misiorowski was set to start game on Wednesday, which complicated the decision somewhat, but there's one guaranteed way to avoid having to worry about Game 5: win game four with three outs to go. After the game, Murphy explained his thought process on going to Drohan over his young ace. Which, uh, wasn't great. As for game five, Murphy added that it's now "all hands on deck" for Milwaukee. "Yeah, it’s all hands on deck," he said. "You can write it up and hope that they perform like the back of their baseball card, but that doesn’t always happen. You go with what you believe is the deal. I trust our guys. I trust them. They put themselves in a position to win." Here's the problem with that: you don't need all hands on deck if you win Game 4. One is that Drohan, any reliever, really, has a very high likelihood of getting three outs against Liam Hicks, Jonny DeLuca and Chandler Simpson. The other? You're three outs from winning the World Series, and you have arguably the best pitcher on the planet available to finish the game. It's not worth worrying about tomorrow, or rest, or injury risk if you win the World Series that's right in front of you. Yes, it would be out of Misiorowski's comfort zone, but the downside was exactly what happened. Instead of scheduling your parade for downtown Milwaukee this weekend, you're going to Game 5. Instead of a title, Milwaukee is now facing a bit more uncertainty. Murphy forgot the golden rule of World Series baseball: flags fly forever.

articles.title: Milwaukee Brewers defeat Tampa Bay Rays to claim first World Series title
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers’ 57-season wait for a World Series title ended Wednesday as they defeated the Tampa Bay Rays in five games.
articles.body: The Milwaukee Brewers’ 57-season wait for a World Series title ended Wednesday as their victory over Tampa Bay completed one of the most dominant postseason runs in MLB history. Once closer Trevor Megill induced a soft ground ball for the last out and their 4-1 win over the Rays in Game 5 was final, the Brewers rushed up the steps of their dugout and onto the playing field at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida. The celebration had been in the making for more than half a century. “This is one of the greatest moments of my life,” Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt said on Fox after the game. “Oh my gosh. It doesn’t even feel real. This is surreal.” After having relocated from Seattle to Milwaukee and played for the first time as the Brewers in 1970, the team didn’t make the World Series until 1982, when it lost in seven games. It then waited 44 years to make its return to the Fall Classic. For a franchise starved for big moments, this year’s team supplied one after another. The Brewers’ 12-2 postseason record is among the best since the MLB postseason format expanded in 1995 to include wild-card teams. The Brewers’ .857 winning percentage was just off the percentages produced by the 1999 New York Yankees and the 2005 Chicago White Sox, which each went 11-1 en route to their own titles. “I don’t even have words,” star pitcher Jacob Misiorowski, who threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings of the clinching game, told Fox after the Game 5 win. Milwaukee is MLB’s smallest market. Its payroll ranked only 19th out of 30 teams. In 12 postseason games, it trailed nine times. But the Brewers won seven of those games by finding ways to prevail in multiple ways. Milwaukee hit seven home runs in a National League Championship Series sweep of the Los Angeles Dodgers yet took a 3-0 series lead on Tampa Bay while hitting just one homer. In Game 5, Milwaukee drove in runs using two singles, a sacrifice fly and a double. Down to its final out in the bottom of the ninth inning, Tampa Bay got on the board when Chandler Simpson’s two-out double drove in Liam Hicks to trim the deficit to 4-1. With hard-throwing reliever Aaron Ashby waiting to relieve Megill in case he got into any more trouble, a soft grounder ended the game. Catcher William Contreras earned Most Valuable Player honors after driving in four runs and hitting .381 during the World Series. “I don’t have words to say,” Contreras said through a translator. This was no fluke by a scrappy team that got hot at the right time. Milwaukee had the second-best record in baseball at July’s All-Star break and ultimately won an MLB-high and franchise-record 103 games. After it beat San Diego in the divisional round, it swept two-time reigning champion Los Angeles in the National League Championship Series. Even though the Dodgers’ payroll was more than double the Brewers’, Milwaukee scored 10 more runs over the sweep to secure a World Series berth against Tampa Bay. The Rays were in some ways a mirror image of Milwaukee, another light-spending franchise looking to turn its regular-season success — the Rays had won the most games in the American League — into its first World Series victory. “Best feeling ever,” Christian Yelich, the Brewers’ captain, said on the broadcast. After one-run wins in the first two games of the World Series — including a Game 2 comeback in which Milwaukee fell behind 4-0 in the first inning — it won Game 3 in a 10-1 rout sparked by Christian Yelich’s stolen base in the fifth inning. When a challenge ruled Yelich safe at second base, Milwaukee proceeded to score eight runs with two outs, blowing the game open without ever hitting a home run. Milwaukee’s championship run was possible thanks to a dependable core of players who spanned generations. Yelich, 34, and 33-year-old reliever Brandon Woodruff, whose save in Game 3 was his first appearance since July 4 because of injuries, were the only players remaining from a 2018 Brewers roster that was just one win away from that season’s World Series. In the divisional round against San Diego, 20-year-old outfielder Jackson Chourio hit a late two-run homer that saved Milwaukee in its opening game of the postseason. Chourio then delivered a walk-off single to win the following game. On the mound, Milwaukee constructed a feared rotation of arms starting with Misiorowski, the 24-year-old with blazing speed who made the All-Star Game as a rookie in 2025 after just five starts. For his encore, Misiorowski in 2026 led a pitching staff that allowed MLB’s second-lowest team ERA during the regular season. When he left games, a bullpen with arms just as nasty and hard-throwing as Misiorowski’s took over. “This is just incredible,” Megill, on the mound for the final out, said after the win. “Ten-year-old me would be so proud.” All of the pieces worked, all season. When the regular season ended, Milwaukee stood alone at the top of the standings. And when the playoffs ended a month later, the Brewers were on top yet again. Their long wait for a title had ended.

articles.title: MLB Has a New Formula for Winning the World Series
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions for the first time in franchise history on Wednesday night, closing out the Tampa Bay Rays to cap off a dominant 11-2 postseason run.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions for the first time in franchise history on Wednesday night, closing out the Tampa Bay Rays to cap off a dominant 11-2 postseason run.

In an era defined by the haves and have-nots in payroll flexibility, and with the free-spending Los Angeles Dodgers winning back-to-back titles, the Brewers have shown there's another way.

Limitless spending is simply not an option for all 30 teams, and while the new CBA could level the playing field a bit, small and major markets will still exist.

The Brewers ranked 19th in the majors with a $134.4 million luxury tax payroll, roughly $250 million less than the Dodgers team they sent packing with a four-game sweep in the NLCS.

So how did they do it? And how can your team be the next Brewers?

It all starts with their offensive style of play, which runs counter to today's power-centric, three-true-outcomes game that so many teams lean on.

The Brewers ranked second in the majors in runs scored (832) during the regular season, but tied for 28th in home runs (154). Rather than living and dying by the long ball, they manufactured runs, led the league with a .341 team on-base percentage and ranked fifth in stolen bases.

Their ability to string together hits and put crooked numbers on the scoreboard was on full display in Game 3 of the World Series, when they plated 10 runs without hitting a ball over the fence. The peak moment came in the fifth inning, when six consecutive two-out hits drove in runs.

They were also one of the league's best defensive teams, rarely giving up extra-base hits and committing just 72 errors in 162 games.

Second baseman Brice Turang is the perfect example of a well-rounded player who fits the organization's philosophy.

He's not a 30-homer slugger, but a 7.3-WAR player, thanks to his on-base ability (.366 OBP) and elite defense (23 DRS, 14 OAA) as a former NL Platinum Glove winner.

The 26-year-old is not the traditional face-of-the-franchise superstar, but that gaudy 7.3 WAR trailed only Pete Crow-Armstrong (9.8) and Cristopher Sánchez (8.1) among all players across baseball.

He is also a homegrown talent, which brings us to another key component of what the Brewers have built.

In an era when analytics and video are at the forefront of how teams evaluate talent, the Brewers are proving traditional in-person scouting can still provide a legitimate competitive edge.

"For teams on a more limited baseball operations budget, investments in infrastructure are seen as more stable and reliable uses of resources than lavish free-agent spending on players who could get hurt or regress," wrote Anthony Castrovince of MLB.com while highlighting how well both of this year's pennant winners balance analytics and old-school scouting.

The Brewers had 64 scouting department members listed in this year's media guide, one of the largest groups in baseball. Both of this year's World Series teams had the maximum six scouts present to watch the opposing LCS matchup, a rare sight as teams lean harder into video scouting.

That dedication to finding a behind-the-scenes advantage has also stretched into the club's player development pipeline, and a quick glance at all the homegrown talent on the World Series roster shows what an important component that has been to the organization's success.

SP Jacob Misiorowski LF Jackson Chourio 2B Brice Turang RP Aaron Ashby SP Logan Henderson CF Garrett Mitchell SS Cooper Pratt RP Abner Uribe RF Sal Frelick

Without that group, which cost $26.3 million in combined salaries in 2026, the Brewers would not be World Series champions.

And the well hasn't run dry. They still have what is widely regarded as a top-10 farm system, headlined by infielder Jesús Made, who will be a strong contender to start the 2027 season as baseball's No. 1 prospect.

While some teams treat their farm system as trade fodder or block their rising talent with high-priced free agents, the Brewers' philosophy is built more on opportunity for those players.

In fact, the Brewers have made a point of trading away some of their top established talent before they hit the open market and lose value as two-month rentals.

Freddy Peralta, Devin Williams, Corbin Burnes and Josh Hader were all traded when their value was still high, despite the fact that the Brewers were actively trying to contend. They also let shortstop Willy Adames walk in free agency, even though many teams would have paid a premium to keep a team leader, and his first two seasons in San Francisco on a seven-year, $182 million deal have fallen flat.

Through all that high-profile turnover, the organization has not missed a beat.

Every time those trades happen, the initial takeaway is that the Brewers aren't doing enough to win now. Then they go out and do just that.

Give yourself enough chances, and things will eventually click in October.

With four straight NL Central division titles and eight playoff appearances in the last nine years, this was not a team finally arriving. This team had a seat at the table for almost a decade, finally got over the hump, and when reaching the postseason is half the battle, that level of sustainability matters.

The Brewers have built something that can endure a shifting MLB landscape, and they've done it using tools that are readily available to all 30 MLB franchises—a cohesive philosophy, a dedication to player development and a pipeline of homegrown talent.

They might not have the highest ceiling in baseball every season, but their consistently high floor has become their edge, and it finally led to a World Series title in 2026.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Brewers catcher William Contreras wins MVP thanks to big effort with his bat and behind the plate
articles.summary: The Brewers capped a historic season and a dominant postseason run with a 4-1 win over the Rays to secure the first championship in franchise history.
articles.body:
Milwaukee Brewers catcher William Contreras is the World Series MVP.

The Brewers' veteran helped lead Milwaukee to the franchise's first World Series championship via a dominant effort with his bat and a standout performance behind the plate. He fought back tears after being named MVP at the conclusion of Milwaukee's 4-1 Game 5 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday , which secured a 4-1 series victory.

"I don't have words to say for how I'm feeling," Contreras said after winning the award.

In five World Series games, Contreras slashed .381/.435/.429 with 2 walks, 4 RBI, 2 runs scored and 1 stolen base. He hit an RBI single in the first inning of Game 1 to spot Milwaukee a 2-0 lead in what ended up being a 3-2 win.

In the sixth inning of Wednesday's decisive Game 5, Contreras knocked in a run with a double and came around to score as the Brewers took control with a 4-0 lead.

Contreras was in control behind the plate throughout the series, as Milwaukee's pitching staff muted a hot-hitting Rays lineup, limiting Tampa Bay to 2.4 runs per game. He also set the defensive tone in Milwaukee's Game 1 win, with two caught stealings to end Rays threats.

In that one, Contreras threw Victor Mesa Jr. out at third base to end the top of the fifth with leadoff hitter Yandy Díaz at the plate. Contreras then threw Jonathan Aranda out at second to end the top of the sixth and maintain Milwaukee's 2-1 lead.

Several Brewers gave Contreras a run for MVP

Contreras topped a competitive MVP race in which as many as five Brewers had a solid case for the award.

Jackson Chourio was Milwaukee's best hitter in the series, with a .458/.458/.542 slash line and 11 total hits. His 10 hits through Game 4 tied him with Babe Ruth for the most in the first four games in World Series history.

Rookie Cooper Pratt was Milwaukee's most productive hitter, with a .421/.455/.684 slash line with 1 home run and 7 RBI. His run of six consecutive hits across Games 4 and 5 set a World Series record for a rookie.

Reliever Aaron Ashby capped one of the most dominant bullpen efforts in MLB postseason history with 5 2/3 scoreless innings across three appearances in the World Series. He finished the postseason with 18 scoreless innings across nine appearances, the most ever by a reliever in a single postseason .

And ace Jacob Misiorowski pitched 10 2/3 one-run innings across two Fall Classic starts, securing wins in Games 1 and 5. He threw 5 2/3 shutout innings to lead Milwaukee to victory on Wednesday.

But in the end, it was Contreras who earned the hardware. It was a fitting honor for the three-time All-Star, who has been with the Brewers since their run of four consecutive playoff appearances began in 2023.

The Brewers capped their historic season and a dominant postseason run with Wednesday's victory to secure the first championship in franchise history .

They led baseball with 103 wins in the regular season. Then they beat the San Diego Padres in four games in the NLDS to set up a rematch in the NLCS with a two-time reigning champion Los Angeles Dodgers team that swept them in last year's NLCS.

The Brewers proceeded to dispatch the Dodgers with a four-game sweep and needed just five games to beat the AL champion Rays. They lost two playoff games en route to their long-awaited title and finish the postseason 11-2.

There was little doubt this postseason about which team is the best in baseball, and the Brewers will return to Milwaukee to celebrate with their fans with the franchise's first championship parade.

articles.title: William Contreras Wins 2026 World Series MVP Award Over Cooper Pratt After Brewers Beat Rays
articles.summary: William Contreras was named MVP of the 2026 World Series as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays with a 4-1 victory in Game 5 on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
William Contreras was named MVP of the 2026 World Series as the Milwaukee Brewers defeated the Tampa Bay Rays with a 4-1 victory in Game 5 on Wednesday night.

With the win, the Brewers captured their first World Series title in franchise history.

Contreras was impressive throughout the Fall Classic, hitting .381 with an OPS of .864 during the series. He picked up four RBI in five games.

The 28-year-old earned World Series MVP honors over Cooper Pratt, who slashed .421/.455/.684 against Tampa Bay.

Pratt was particularly stellar at the plate throughout the final two games of the series, putting together a streak of six consecutive at-bats with a hit.

The award ultimately went to Contreras, who also made his presence felt defensively as Milwaukee took down Tampa Bay.

The Rays led the American League with 164 stolen bases in the regular season, but struggled against Contreras. He caught them stealing four times in nine attempts during the World Series.

He was also sharp behind the plate, winning 10 of his 13 Automated Ball-Strike (ABS) challenges (h/t Johnny Flores Jr. of The Athletic).

Contreras has served as a crucial piece of Milwaukee's lineup throughout his four years with the organization, earning two of his three All-Star nods as a member of the Brewers.

During the 2026 regular season, he hit .270 while racking up 18 home runs, 27 doubles and 94 RBI. Contreras stepped up for Milwaukee in the playoffs, recording three homers and nine RBI to go along with a 1.036 OPS in 13 games.

Now, he can add World Series MVP to his résumé.

articles.title: World Series 2026: Brewers beat Rays in Game 5 to win first title in franchise's 57-year history
articles.summary: The Brewers completed an 11-2 postseason run with a complete team victory in Game 5 of the World Series.
articles.body: A 57-year wait is over. The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions for the first time in franchise history.The Brewers completed a dominant postseason run on Wednesday with a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays, winning the 2026 Fall Classic in five games after falling just short of a sweep in Game 4.The decisive game looked like plenty of other Brewers wins. A shutout start by presumptive NL Cy Young Award winner Jacob Misiorowski, who exited only due to cramps. A calm night for an elite bullpen. Production from up and down a pesky and patient lineup.The result ultimately felt inevitable, with every Milwaukee player once again executing their specific job until second baseman Brice Turang threw out Richie Palacios to end the game — and the 2026 MLB season.THERE IT IS! The final out!The @Brewers are your 2026 World Series Champions@MLBONFOX pic.twitter.com/9z890xay2o— FOX Sports (@FOXSports) October 29, 2026 Catcher William Contreras was named World Series MVP, but he might as well have received the award for being the best player of the postseason. The three-time All-Star slashed.373/.448/.588 in 13 games while throwing out six of 13 baserunners and winning 21 of 31 ABS challenges.In the World Series, he hit 8-for-21 (.381) with four RBI, including one on a double in Game 5.WILD BILL PLATES THE CAPTAIN William Contreras puts the Brewers up 3-0 🔥 pic.twitter.com/TabXzkhwAe— MLB (@MLB) October 29, 2026 The Rays were trying to become the first team to come back from down 3-0 in a World Series, and they would have made history just by sending the series back to Milwaukee. No team that fell down 3-0 in the World Series has ever forced a Game 6.In total, the Brewers went 11-2 this postseason, and their only two losses were to teams trying to avoid sweeps. They won eight straight games from Game 4 of the NLDS through Game 3 of the World Series, tying an MLB postseason record.The list of title-less MLB teams is now down to four: the San Diego Padres, Colorado Rockies, Seattle Mariners and, of course, the Rays. The Brewers had been tied with San Diego for the oldest team in the league without a title but no more.This is, however, not the first World Series title in the city of Milwaukee's history, as the Milwaukee Braves won it all in 1957, eight years before they moved to their current home in Atlanta and 13 years before the Brewers came to town after a single season as the Seattle Pilots.The Brewers had reason to be confident in Game 5The Brewers would've certainly preferred to end the series on Tuesday, which would have made them the first team in MLB history to sweep both the championship series and the World Series. The Rays, however, pulled off an out-of-nowhere win in 12 innings.That victory came with a cost. The Rays used every premium arm available to them, as well as presumed Game 5 starter Nick Martinez, who threw 33 pitches and then wasn't available Wednesday. The Brewers, meanwhile, had Misiorowski waiting with a relatively rested bullpen.In Game 5, the Rays started ace Drew Rasmussen on short rest, being aggressive with a pitcher they tried to get extra rest as much as possible during the regular season. Rasmussen wound up throwing four innings but surrendered the first run on a single by Cooper Pratt, who set a World Series rookie record with six straight hits across Games 4 and 5.Cooper Pratt strikes again 🤯He's 5 for his last 6 and gets the Brewers on the board here in Game 5! pic.twitter.com/lSGfvdamUQ— MLB (@MLB) October 29, 2026 More Brewers runs arrived in the fifth and sixth innings, upping the degree of difficulty for the Rays into untenable territory. Two of those runs were driven in by Pratt and No. 9 hitter David Hamilton, marking the latest damage from the bottom of the Brewers' order.In total, the Brewers' Nos. 7, 8 and 9 hitters went 17-for-59 in the series, with nine runs scored and 12 RBI. The team scored 24 runs total. The bottom of the order delivered the Brewers' only three homers of the series.Meanwhile, the only thing that really went wrong in Misiorowski's start was that his calf started cramping in the sixth inning. That brought an abrupt end to his best start of the postseason — 5 2/3 shutout innings, 2 hits, 2 strikeouts — and he finished Milwaukee's playoff run with a 1.89 ERA, not far off from his 1.80 mark in the regular season.Jacob Misiorowski is FIRED UP after finishing his 5th scoreless inning with a strikeout pic.twitter.com/DZ6i2t0WRC— FOX Sports: MLB (@MLBONFOX) October 29, 2026 Once Misiorowski was out Wednesday, the Brewers' bullpen took over. JoJo Romero got two outs without incident. Abner Uribe got two outs without incident. Closer Trevor Megill got called in for a two-inning save and did allow the Rays' only run on an RBI double by Chandler Simpson in the ninth.Four pitches later, the game was over.The only surprising relief choice was the lack of Aaron Ashby, one of the breakout stars of the postseason. The left-hander was warming as Megill faced Palacios but didn't enter the game after throwing 2 1/3 innings and 31 pitches the previous night.How will these Brewers be remembered?The 2026 Brewers were a team with a clear identity, built on a marriage of new-school analytics and old-school methods they brought back into vogue. They bunted, stole bases, mostly eschewed homers (none in Game 5), emphasized defense and regularly used multi-inning relievers. They also walked more than any other team, pulled their starters early and featured a pitcher with a fastball that has touched 105 mph.It was all executed on a small-market budget by manager Pat Murphy and president of baseball operations Matt Arnold, creating the kind of winner not often seen in modern baseball. It took relentless iteration, as shown by what happens when you rewind to the 2023 Brewers, a 92-win team that won the first of four straight NL Central titles.Corbin Burnes was the staff ace, having won the Cy Young Award in 2021. The No. 2 pitcher was Freddy Peralta. The closer was Devin Williams. Willy Adames led the Brewers in home runs at shortstop. Craig Counsell was manager. David Stearns was still in the building, advising ownership after a tenure as the whiz kid president of baseball operations.All those people left or were traded. Burnes was dealt to the Baltimore Orioles ahead of the 2024 season, before he could leave in free agency. Williams was traded ahead of the 2025 season, before he could leave in free agency. Peralta was traded last offseason, before he could leave in free agency. Adames left in free agency. Counsell left for the Cubs, the NL Central rivals. Stearns went home to New York to run the Mets.And yet, the Brewers persevered, finding and developing even more talent until they became World Series champions.When will we next see baseball?Milwaukee is undeniably a feel-good story, but this team's breakthrough comes with a sour note.It can be plainly said that we don't know when the next MLB game will be played. The 2027 season opener is scheduled for March 24, but that's merely a date on a calendar. Much more real is the upcoming labor fight between MLB's 30 owners and the MLB Players Assocation.The owners have made it clear that they want a salary cap like the NFL, NBA and NHL have. The players have made that a nonstarter for decades and went as far as striking to avoid a cap in 1994. The owners are already preparing for a lockout, and there's no telling how long that will go with both sides completely dug in.It will likely be an ugly offseason. Fans can only hope there's at least a 2027 season after that.

articles.title: Cooper Pratt sets rookie World Series record with sixth consecutive hit as Brewers top Rays for first title
articles.summary: The Brewers beat the Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to claim the franchise's first World Series title.
articles.body:
Cooper Pratt made history on Wednesday as his team lifted the Commissioner's Trophy.

The Milwaukee Brewers' shortstop became the first rookie to record six consecutive hits in the World Series. He had two hits in the Brewers' 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5 on Wednesday, which secured the franchise's first World Series title .

"This is one of the greatest moments of my life," an emotional Pratt said on Fox after the win. "Oh, my gosh. It doesn't even feel real. … It's some of the hardest and most fun baseball I've ever been a part of."

After going 0-for-1 to start Game 4 on Tuesday, Pratt rattled off four hits in his final four at-bats, including what was almost a game-winning home run in the 12th inning .

The Brewers' shortstop then tallied two hits Wednesday, with a single to left in the fifth inning earning him the record.

Pratt's first Game 5 hit was an RBI single to center that scored Brice Turang and gave Milwaukee an early 1-0 lead. That hit was his fifth consecutive, tying him for the previous rookie World Series record with Brian Doyle, who registered five consecutive hits in the 1978 World Series.

Pratt fouled out in his third at-bat of Game 5, which brought his hitting streak to an end. But he still drove in a run, which gave the Brewers a 4-0 lead in the sixth.

Game 4 on Tuesday went into extra innings, and Pratt was nearly the hero for Milwaukee. He launched a 396-foot home run to left-center to give the Brewers a 3-2 lead in the top of the 12th. But Tampa Bay came back in the bottom of the inning to force Game 5.

The home run was only the fourth of Pratt's MLB career and his first of the postseason.

The 22-year-old rookie debuted for Milwaukee on June 16, going 0-for-3 in his first game. Over the rest of the regular season, the shortstop played in 74 games and slashed .281/.350/.368 with three home runs and 34 RBI. Pratt also stole 19 bases.

Milwaukee's shortstop was a singles machine in the regular season. He tallied 64 hits, and only 12 of them went for extra bases.

Pratt finishes the World Series 8-for-19, with a home run and seven RBI. He's the first rookie to record seven RBI over a four-game span in the World Series since 1919.

Pratt's World Series performance made him a contender for MVP. He didn't end up winning that honor — William Contreras won it instead — but Pratt is headed home with a ring just a few months after his MLB debut.

articles.title: Brewers Parade 2026 Date, Route, Time, Anticipated Crowd and Latest Info After World Series Title
articles.summary: It's time to party, Milwaukee.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers clinched their first World Series title in franchise history Wednesday with a 4-1 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5. When the dust settles on their celebration in Tampa, they will shift their attention toward what figures to be a memorable homecoming in Milwaukee.

Brewers fans won't have to wait long for the ensuing parade, as USA Today's Bob Nightengale reported it will take place Friday in downtown Milwaukee.

The parade will start on Wisconsin Avenue and make its way toward the lakefront. Nightengale noted there are expected to be at least 400,000 people in attendance.

Such a large crowd is anything but surprising, as Brewers fans took over Tropicana Field during the World Series.

"It's been awesome to see," Christian Yelich said of the crowd support, per Nightengale. "It's been pretty evident this month about how much the fans have gotten behind this team, the fan support that we've had at the road venues, at our home ballpark."

Milwaukee jumped out to a commanding 3-0 lead in the series but gave some of the momentum back when the Rays won Game 4 in extra innings.

Yet ace Jacob Misiorowski made sure that momentum was short-lived when he took the mound Wednesday for what proved to be the decisive contest. He allowed just two hits in 5.2 shutout innings before exiting with a calf cramp .

Fortunately for the right-hander, the Milwaukee bullpen continued its postseason dominance by allowing just one run the rest of the way. Offensively, Cooper Pratt went 2-for-3 with two RBI, while World Series MVP William Contreras drove in another run.

There were so many postseason heroes for the Brewers along the way, and the fans will get to celebrate them all Friday.

articles.title: Brewers’ Aaron Ashby caps 2026 postseason with bonkers ERA

articles.body:
Whenever Aaron Ashby would make his way to the mound from the Milwaukee Brewers bullpen, opposing hitters may as well head back to the dugout and not even attempt to hit against him. That's how good Ashby has been over the course of the 2026 MLB postseason.

The Brewers may not have needed Ashby to work his usual magic for them to take a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 5 of the World Series and close things out, but the lefty has done more than enough to put Milwaukee in a position to get over the hump.

Ashby appeared in nine of the Brewers' 13 postseason games and shut the door on every single occasion. He allowed just five hits and walked three in 18 innings pitched while striking out 20. And perhaps most importantly, opponents did not score a single run on him throughout the entire postseason, giving him a 2026 postseason ERA of 0.00, as pointed out by FOX Sports MLB on X.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

There was no doubt that Ashby had grown into Brewers manager Pat Murphy's most trusted relief pitcher. If Trevor Megill ended up allowing another base hit and another run in the bottom of the ninth, he would have deployed Ashby to close things out against the Rays.

Ashby has been clutch all season long, coming in whenever the Brewers needed him to put out fires or protect leads. In the regular season, he appeared in 75 games, pitched 89.1 innings, and earned 13 wins despite making just one start, finishing the campaign with a 3.12 ERA.

He's a true homegrown talent for the Brewers; Milwaukee drafted him in the fourth round back in 2018, and he didn't stick in the starting rotation, carving out a niche for himself as a shutdown reliever instead. It's an incredible rise from Ashby, especially when he missed the entire 2023 season due to a shoulder injury.

Everyone did their part for the Brewers in their World Series-winning run, but Ashby deserves his flowers for always rising to the occasion when the team would call upon his name.

articles.title: No World Series miracle for weary Rays
articles.summary: After defying expectations with an American League-best 98 regular-season wins, sweeping the New York Yankees and besting Cleveland, the Tampa Bay Rays endur...
articles.body:
After defying expectations with an American League-best 98 regular-season wins, sweeping the New York Yankees and besting Cleveland, the Tampa Bay Rays endured an all-too familiar World Series finish.

The Milwaukee Brewers polished off a four-games-to-one victory over the Rays in Major League Baseball's championship showcase on Wednesday, leaving manager Kevin Cash "crushed" but grateful for the latest ride.

"It's a special group," he said of the Rays. "They're banged up and hurting right now, but just grateful for the way they carried themselves all season long, winning a bunch of games. It's as close knit of a group as I've ever been around."

After dropping the first three games to the Brewers the Rays rallied in extra innings in game four to stay alive.

With the season still on the line on Wednesday pitching ace Drew Rasmussen took the ball on just three days' rest.

"We knew it was a big ask," Cash said. "But appreciate Drew Rasmussen so much for taking the ball, wanting the ball and going out and doing what he did."

Rasmussen allowed just one run over four innings, but the worn-out relief corps couldn't keep the Brewers in check.

In addition, the Rays scored just 12 runs over the five games, going eight-for-39 at the plate with runners in scoring position.

"Milwaukee Brewers pitching, it's as simple as that," Cash said of what caused the Rays' struggles at the plate.

Some Rays players stayed in the dugout to watch as the Brewers celebrated the first World Series title in franchise history.

"If it's something that you log in the back of your mind that, you know, you want to experience that, we want to experience that real soon here in the coming seasons," Cash said. "If it's better for that person or that individual that chose to sit and watch it, I can appreciate that."

The Rays remain without a World Series title, having also come up short in 2008 and 2020. But even in the midst of the disappointment Cash said he was excited by the idea of what a returning core of Rays players could do next season.

"Speaking of the guys who contributed to this postseason run, it's very easy to be excited, remain excited about the quality of players and people that we have coming," he said.

articles.title: World Series 2026: 10 wild stats from the Brewers' first title
articles.summary: There has never been a team quite like the 2026 Brewers.
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are your 2026 World Series champions, having capped off a dominant postseason with a 4-1 win over the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday .

It's a cathartic night for the Brewers, who were previously tied with the San Diego Padres as the oldest MLB team to have never won a World Series title. They are now permanently off that list , thanks to a team that leveraged its strengths all years.

How did the Brewers do it? Let's dive into that via numbers.

We're going to go ahead and list off every starting pitcher the Brewers faced in their 12 postseason games: Robbie Ray, Michael King, Nick Pivetta, Walker Buehler, Tarik Skubal, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tyler Glasnow, Nick Martinez, Drew Rasmussen and Freddy Peralta.

That his a formidable group, even by playoff standards. Combined, they have 15 total All-Star appearances (and five Cy Young awards) compared to the Brewers rotation's two, both by Jacob Misiorowski. And even Misiorowski's first All-Star appearance last year was a matter of some controversy .

Would you like to know how long that group lasted against the Brewers lineup on average?

It's 4.2 innings. Only one pitcher lasted longer than five innings at all and it was surprisingly Snell, despite the Los Angeles Dodgers left-hander being infamous for short starts even while posting zeroes.

The Brewers chased nearly every pitcher they faced this postseason by doing what they did all regular season. No team swung less at pitches. No team drew more walks. Only two teams in MLB missed less often when they did swing. They hit the most ground balls and the most balls to the opposite field.

They didn't hit home runs much, ranking only 29th in MLB, but that entire previous paragraph turned their offense into a torture device for even some of MLB's best pitchers.

Funnily enough, the Brewers starters lasted just as long as those opponents this postseason at 4.2 innings per start, but for very different reasons (and that number goes up to 4.5 when you take out Shane Drohan's one-inning appearance as an opener).

The Brewers starters were definitely solid this postseason, but Milwaukee removed them as early as possible in basically every game and roll out its comically dominant bullpen.

The Brewers relievers pitched 65 innings this postseason and posted a 1.38 ERA and a .173 batting average against, per MLB.com's Sarah Langs .

That was the Brewers's formula when you zoom out as much as possible: force the other team's starter out early and turn the game into a battle of the bullpens. It worked to perfection.

There's something to be said, though, about what that means for baseball. The starting pitcher who regularly goes seven innings or more in a start is bordering on extinction. Sandy Alcantara led all pitchers with 214 innings during the regular season, which would have ranked for ninth in MLB 10 years ago and 22nd in MLB 20 years ago.

Teams are now perfectly willing to accept a five-inning start, if it means those are five good innings. This has been a slow shift in MLB for years, but the Brewers just brought it into sharp focus.

That's the proportion of innings the Brewers bullpen covered during the postseason.

That makes Milwaukee the fourth champion in MLB history to get a majority of its innings from relievers, joining the 2020 Los Angeles Dodgers, 2021 Atlanta Braves and 2024 Dodgers.

It had never happened before 2020, another sign of the aggressive-bullpen era. The closest any team ever got before that was the 1960 Pittsburgh Pirates, though that was hardly a conscious decision. That team took three double-digit losses to the New York Yankees before winning in seven games, with relievers forced to cover for short starts in each defeat.

That is the number of home runs hit in the 2026 World Series, per ESPN , the fewest since the 1985 Fall Classic between the Kansas City Royals and St. Louis Cardinals.

The Brewers had three of those homers, from perhaps the three players you would least expect: Sal Frelick, Cooper Pratt and David Hamilton, the No. 6, 7 and 9 hitters in the Game 5 lineup.

The Brewers built their offense around not needing homers to punish pitchers, but they still out-homered the competition in every round, with a total margin of 13 to 4.

In another world, the 2026 World Series ends in Game 4 on Tuesday as a Brewers sweep and rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt gets remembered as the guy who homered his club to its first title.

A 12th-inning collapsed prevented that from coming to pass, but it did give the 22-year-old a chance to make some history. With two more hits in Game 5, Pratt became the first rookie to post a base hit in six straight at-bats in the World Series .

Pratt made his MLB debut in June and was playing high school baseball only three years ago, with the Brewers taking him in the sixth round of the 2023 MLB Draft. He rocketed to the majors thanks to his well-regarded glove, then made his mark with his bat.

With a single in the seventh inning, Brewers star Jackson Chourio became MLB's all-time leader in postseason hits before turning 23, breaking a tie with Andruw Jones with his 31st hit.

Jones posted his 30 hits in 45 games for the Atlanta Braves. Chourio posted his 31 in 25 games. He also tied some guy named Babe Ruth for the most hits in the first four games of a World Series , and now has the second-most in five games behing only Pepper Martin in 1931 .

You would think with either of the above stats, Pratt or Chourio would have been named World Series MVP. It's a sign of how thoroughly great William Contreras was that neither were.

Contreras earned MVP after a postseason in which he was basically the best player in baseball. The three-time All-Star slashed .373/.448/.588 at the plate during the postseason. He threw out 6-of-13 baserunners. And he won won 21 out of 31 ABS challenges (67.8%) in the first postseason with the system, with accuracy and decisiveness becoming a running joke in the Fox Sports booth.

In the World Series, Contreras hit 8-for-21 (.381) with four RBI, including one on a double in Game 5.

What else could you possible want from a catcher?

Misiorowski began the World Series by throwing the fastest pitch in its tracked history at 103.5 mph . He would go on to throw 89 pitches of at least 100 mph between his starts in Games 1 and 5.

Misiorowski didn't reach the end of the sixth inning in either start — exiting Game 5 due to calf cramps — but he allowed only one run in 10 2/3 total innings. His five strikeouts were lower than his regular season norm, but he was still an ace by Brewers standards.

Aaron Ashby went from a relatively anonymous set-up man to the most feared reliever in baseball over the course of the postseason, making nine appearances in 12 games and pitching multiple innings in all but one.

The left-hander didn't allow a single run in his 18 innings pitched, the most innings a reliever has ever thrown in a postseason without giving up a run . He didn't factor into Game 5 after experiencing diminished velocity in a long Game 4 appearance, but he had already contributed more than enough.

There will be plenty of analysis about what it means the Brewers — a classic small-market, big-brain team — winning the World Series means for baseball.

Their $142 million payroll, as estimated by Roster Resource , ranked 19th in MLB this season, right between the Kansas City Royals and Cincinnati Reds. They were actually the financial heavyweight this series, as the Rays ranked 28th at $90 million, followed by their ALCS opponent Cleveland Guardians at $87 million.

You build a champion on that budget with smart decisions and long-term planning. The highest-paid player on the 2026 Brewers was Christian Yelich ($26 million), still playing on the mega-deal he got from his MVP days, followed by the mostly injured Brandon Woodruff ($22 million) and two trade deadline acquisitions in Dustin May and Antonio Senzatela ($12 million each).

No other player on the Brewers made more than $10 million this year. Chourio and Pratt, both 22-year-olds who just starred on a World Series team, are both under team control through at least 2031, at the cost of around $132 million.

Conteras will be back next year on a $14.5 million club option. Nearly every other big contributor is under contract beyond 2027, save for NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, a pending free agent. And let's not forget the Brewers still ranked third in MLB Pipeline's farm system rankings after the trade deadline , with a group headlined by No. 1 overall prospect Jesús Made.

The Brewers were incredible this year. There is every reason to believe they will stay incredible for years to come.
